title: The chariot
theme: Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «ऋतपं संसारिणं», the transmigrant who ‘drinks’; Raṅgarāmānuja: «शरीराधिष्ठातारं»

words.meaning: the owner of the chariot, the rider

sandhi.rule: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
Final m stays m before a vowel.
Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
Final m stays m before a vowel.

morphology.note: rathin, ‘one who has a chariot’, formed from ratha with the possessive suffix -in; Śaṅkara: its owner, «रथस्वामिनं». The vishvAsa mūla keys रथितं, a witness error (corrections.json).
Imperative second person singular of vid ‘know’, with the ending -dhi.
Neuter s-stem: accusative and nominative singular are alike (manaḥ).

translation.literal: ‘Know the self as the owner of the chariot, and the body as just the chariot; know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as just the reins.’
translation.readable: ‘Know the self as the one who rides in the chariot, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect as the driver, and the mind as the reins.’

anvaya: आत्मानम् रथिनम् विद्धि शरीरम् तु रथम् एव [विद्धि] । बुद्धिम् तु सारथिम् विद्धि मनः च प्रग्रहम् एव [विद्धि] ॥
syntax: Two imperatives (viddhi) each govern a pair of accusatives, the thing and what it is to be known as: ātmānaṃ rathinam, buddhiṃ sārathim; the other two pairs (śarīraṃ ratham, manaḥ pragraham) supply the verb. eva marks the identification.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the self conditioned by its adjuncts, the transmigrant who is fit both for knowledge and for ignorance, «यः उपाधिकृतः संसारी विद्याविद्ययोरधिकृतो मोक्षगमनाय संसारगमनाय च». Raṅgarāmānuja: the one who presides over the body, «शरीराधिष्ठातारं».

beginner: Here begins one of the best-known images in the Upaniṣads. A person is like a chariot on a journey. You yourself are the passenger, the one the journey is for. Your body is the chariot that carries you. Your intellect — the part of you that makes decisions — is the driver. Your mind, which reaches out towards things, is the reins the driver holds. Śaṅkara explains why each fits: the body is pulled along by the senses as a chariot is pulled by horses; almost everything the body does depends on the intellect deciding, as a chariot depends on its driver; and the senses act only when the mind directs them, as horses move when the reins guide them. The next verses complete the picture with the horses and the road.
analogy: A carriage ride: the passenger chooses the destination, but it is the driver and the reins that decide whether the horses get there.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: a chariot is imagined as the means for the conditioned self to travel either to release or to saṃsāra, «तस्य तदुभयगमने साधनो रथः कल्प्यते». The body is the chariot because the senses, like horses yoked to it, pull it; the intellect is the charioteer because nearly all the body’s work is done by the intellect, «सर्वं हि देहगतं कार्यं बुद्धिकर्तव्यमेव प्रायेण»; the mind is the reins, because the senses act when the mind holds them, «मनसा हि प्रगृहीतानि श्रोत्रादीनि करणानि प्रवर्तन्ते रशनयेवाश्वाः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The passage from this verse to 1.3.9, he says, teaches the equipment for reaching Viṣṇu’s highest place beyond the road of saṃsāra, «संसाराध्वपारभूतवैष्णवपरमपदप्राप्तौ परिकरम्». The intellect is the charioteer because the body’s activity depends on decision, «बुद्धिशब्दाध्यवसायाधीनत्वात् देहप्रवृत्ते: तस्याः सारथित्वम्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss the chariot image itself. His text reads ca for tu in the first line (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The rider is the self as conditioned by its adjuncts, the transmigrant, «उपाधिकृतः संसारी»; the chariot is the means by which it travels to release or to saṃsāra.

visistadvaita.text: The rider is the self that presides over the body, «शरीराधिष्ठातारं»; the image teaches the means of reaching Viṣṇu’s highest place.

schools.disagreement: Both agree that the rider is the embodied self; they differ on what that self finally is, and on the goal (for Raṅgarāmānuja, Viṣṇu’s highest place, named at 1.3.9). In our source Madhva prints 1.3.3–1.3.11 without comment and then comments once, marking it ॥ १०-१२ ॥, on the deities who preside over the senses, their objects, the mind and the intellect; he does not gloss the chariot image itself.

parallels.note: The Brahmasūtra refers to this image: ‘what is placed in the simile of the body’.

contemporary.text: The chariot is not a picture of a self at war with its body; every part has a job, and the journey depends on how they work together. The question it puts is who is driving. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: In your own day, what plays the part of the driver, and what of the reins?
reflect.deeper: Why does the image make the intellect, not the self, the driver?
reflect.practice: Before one decision today, pause and ask which part of you is choosing.

flags.note: The vishvAsa mūla keys रथितं (witness error); Madhva’s text reads ca for tu (corrections.json).
